case.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit
case.limits: HathiTrust returned page numbers, not text. A system that can emit passages resembling the originals is not obviously on the same side of that line.
case.holding: Digitising a library of books to enable full-text search and access for print-disabled readers was fair use, and the search function was squarely transformative.

case.why_ai_cites_it: It is the cleanest authority that a complete copy of a copyrighted corpus can be lawful when the resulting system serves a purpose the originals do not, and that no output of the protected expression is required for the use to be fair.

reading.body:
The Second Circuit found that digitizing an entire library to enable full-text search and access for disabled readers was fair use, even though the system made complete copies and could serve purposes beyond the originals.

The court treated the search function itself as transformative use. The HathiTrust system did not primarily expose the protected expression to readers; it enabled discovery and accessibility that the books in their original form could not provide. This distinction matters because it permits wholesale copying when the resulting system's purpose diverges meaningfully from the originals' expressive function.

Current AI litigation relies heavily on this precedent because it establishes that a lawful copying can proceed without requiring the final system to output the protected text. The defense in cases involving large language models invokes this logic: the model is trained on complete texts but produces novel outputs, making it transformative rather than derivative. The court's reasoning suggests the copying itself, not the output, is the legally relevant act.

The holding does not settle whether statistical models trained on copyrighted text occupy the same legal ground as searchable databases of preserved books. It also does not address whether transformative use extends to systems whose outputs closely resemble the originals. The court noted this limit explicitly. The precedent clarifies what fair use can permit, but leaves open how far that permission reaches when the intermediate step of copying is identical but the downstream applications diverge.
